title: Data modeling & databases
blurb: Normalization, keys, NULLs, indexes and loads on the database side; grain, facts and dimensions on the analytical side.

cards.prompt: The one-line test for third normal form.
cards.answer: Every non-key attribute depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.
cards.why: 'The key' is 1NF (rows identified by a key, no repeating groups). 'The whole key' is 2NF (no partial dependency on part of a composite key). 'Nothing but the key' is 3NF (no transitive dependency through another non-key attribute).
cards.source: William Kent, A Simple Guide to Five Normal Forms (1983)

cards.prompt: What problem does normalization solve? Name the three anomalies it prevents.
cards.answer: It stores each fact once, so the data can't contradict itself. It prevents update anomalies (changing a fact in one row but not its copies), insertion anomalies (being unable to record one fact without inventing another), and deletion anomalies (losing one fact when you delete a row about another).
points: Each fact stored once; no self-contradiction
Update anomaly
Insertion anomaly
Deletion anomaly

cards.prompt: When is denormalizing the right call, and what does it cost?
cards.answer: In read-heavy analytical models, where data is loaded in batches and integrity is enforced by the load process rather than by each write. Star schemas deliberately denormalize dimensions. The cost is redundancy that the pipeline must keep consistent. Transactional systems that take many concurrent writes should stay normalized.
points: Read-heavy, batch-loaded analytical workloads
Integrity moves to the load process
Cost: redundancy the pipeline must keep consistent
Keep write-heavy transactional systems normalized

cards.prompt: Surrogate vs natural keys: why do warehouses use meaningless surrogate keys?
cards.answer: Natural keys carry business meaning, so they change, get reused, and arrive formatted differently from different sources. A surrogate key is a stable, meaningless identifier that insulates the model from those changes and makes history tracking (Type 2 dimensions) possible. Keep the natural key as an attribute with a uniqueness rule so you can still look rows up by it.
points: Natural keys change, get reused, vary across sources
Surrogates are stable and meaningless
Surrogates enable Type 2 history
Keep the natural key as a constrained attribute

cards.prompt: Why does `WHERE x NOT IN (SELECT y FROM t)` return no rows when one y is NULL?
cards.answer: SQL uses three-valued logic. Any comparison with NULL is UNKNOWN, not TRUE or FALSE. NOT IN expands to x <> y1 AND x <> y2 AND ..., and one UNKNOWN term makes the whole conjunction UNKNOWN or FALSE, never TRUE. WHERE keeps only TRUE rows. Use NOT EXISTS, or filter out the NULLs.
points: Comparisons with NULL are UNKNOWN
WHERE keeps only TRUE
NOT IN is a chain of <> joined by AND
Use NOT EXISTS or exclude NULLs
cards.source: ISO SQL semantics; any SQL reference

cards.prompt: What does an index cost, and when does it fail to help?
cards.answer: Every insert, update and delete must maintain each index, and indexes take storage. An index helps selective predicates that touch a small fraction of rows. It rarely helps low-selectivity columns (a yes/no flag) or queries that read most of the table. For a composite index, column order matters: it serves queries that filter on its leading columns.
points: Write and storage cost on every change
Helps selective predicates
Little help for low-selectivity columns or full scans
Composite indexes serve their leading columns

cards.prompt: What makes a data load idempotent, and why does it matter?
cards.answer: Running it twice produces the same result as running it once. Common patterns are replacing a whole partition or date range, or merging on keys instead of appending. It matters because loads fail and get retried: a rerun of an append-only load duplicates data, while an idempotent one can be retried safely.
points: Same result whether run once or many times
Replace a partition/range, or merge on keys
Append-only reruns duplicate data
Makes retries and backfills safe

cards.prompt: Kimball's four steps of dimensional design, in order.
cards.answer: 1. Select the business process. 2. Declare the grain. 3. Identify the dimensions. 4. Identify the facts.
cards.source: Kimball & Ross, The Data Warehouse Toolkit, 3rd ed.

cards.prompt: What does 'declare the grain' mean, and what goes wrong if you skip it?
cards.answer: State exactly what one fact row represents, for example one row per order line, or one row per ticket per status change. Skip it and grains get mixed in one table, which causes double counting and measures that are right only at some levels of aggregation.
points: Grain = the business meaning of one row
Declared before dimensions and facts are chosen
Mixed grains lead to double counting and inconsistent measures

cards.prompt: An order moves through placed, paid, shipped and delivered, with one row per order whose milestone dates fill in over time. Which fact-table type?
cards.why: Transaction: one row per event. Periodic snapshot: one row per period (inventory at month end). Accumulating snapshot: one row per process instance, updated as milestones occur. It's the natural home for durations between steps.

cards.prompt: Slowly changing dimension Types 1, 2 and 3, one line each.
cards.answer: Type 1: overwrite (no history). Type 2: add a new row with effective dates and a current flag (full history). Type 3: add a previous-value column (one step of history).

cards.prompt: What are a conformed dimension and a bus matrix, and why do they matter across teams?
cards.answer: A conformed dimension has the same keys and meaning everywhere it is used, such as one Customer, Date or Location dimension. That lets you drill across business processes. A bus matrix lists processes as rows and conformed dimensions as columns. It is the roadmap that keeps separately built models compatible.
points: Same keys and meaning across fact tables
Enables drill-across between processes
Bus matrix = processes by shared dimensions, the integration plan

cards.prompt: Why do columnar analytical engines favor a star schema over one wide flat table or a deep snowflake?
cards.answer: Columnar storage compresses low-cardinality dimension columns well, and dimensions filter facts through simple one-to-many joins. A wide flat table repeats attributes on every row and invites inconsistent measures and grain errors. A deep snowflake adds join hops and confuses the people writing reports.
points: Columnar compression favors low-cardinality dimension columns
Dimensions filter facts via one-to-many joins
Flat tables: repetition, grain errors, inconsistent measures
Snowflakes: extra hops and author confusion
cards.source: Kimball & Ross; BI vendor modeling guidance

cards.prompt: A team wants 'one big flat table' so analysts can self-serve. What do you recommend, and how do you sell it?
cards.answer: Name the risks: mixed grains, double counting, and every report reinventing its measures. Offer a shared semantic model instead: a star schema with a few conformed dimensions and curated, documented measures. One certified model then feeds many reports. Teach people to build on that model rather than their own extracts. Sell it with a before-and-after on their own numbers, ideally a total that comes out differently today depending on who built the report.
points: Name the risks: grain, double counting, inconsistent measures
Propose a shared semantic model (star, conformed dimensions, curated measures)
One certified model feeds many reports
Teach report building on the shared model
Persuade with their own numbers
